title: India Just Logged Its Driest June in Fifteen Years. The Next Two Weeks Will Decide What Millions of Farmers Eat.
excerpt: Kharif sowing is running 23% behind last year, El Niño is strengthening, and food prices are already climbing. The monsoon's July performance will shape inflation and rural incomes for months to come.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • India recorded its driest June in 15 years, impacting agriculture and food prices.
  • Kharif crop planting is 23% behind last year, with soybean down 65% and cotton down 35%.
  • A strengthening El Niño raises concerns for rainfall and agricultural output through 2026.
  • Food prices are rising, with cooking oils up 12-17% and tomatoes up 23% year-on-year.
  • The next two weeks are critical for crop recovery and economic stability for millions.
India just recorded its fifth-driest June since weather records began in 1901 — and the driest in more than a decade. The monsoon season, which normally delivers about 70% of the country's annual rainfall, has stumbled badly. June rainfall came in at 39.8% below the long-term average, leaving vast stretches of farmland parched and pushing the planting of crucial summer crops dangerously behind schedule. The implications ripple far beyond the fields. India's nearly $4-trillion economy depends on the monsoon to replenish reservoirs, recharge groundwater, and sustain an agricultural sector that employs roughly half the population. When the monsoon falters, food prices rise, rural incomes shrink, and millions of families — including those sustained by diaspora remittances — feel the squeeze. For NRIs, this often means increased financial pressure on their families back home, potentially leading to higher remittance needs to cover rising living costs. ## The Sowing Gap Is Already Alarming Data released by the Union Agriculture Ministry on June 29 tells a stark story. Kharif (summer) crop planting across India is running 23% behind last year's pace. The most water-dependent crops have been hit hardest: soybean planting is down a staggering 65%, cotton area has fallen 35%, and rice — India's staple and the backbone of its position as the world's largest rice exporter — is down 25%. Farmers across central and eastern India, the regions worst hit by the rainfall shortfall, have been forced to delay sowing paddy, pulses, cotton, and oilseeds. The Agriculture Ministry has flagged 300 districts as particularly vulnerable due to limited irrigation coverage. For rain-fed crops like tur dal (arhar) and soybean, where irrigation covers barely 11-14% of cultivated area, the stakes are especially high. "Soybean, cotton and tur remain the most weather-sensitive crops, with July rainfall crucial for acreage recovery," warned agricultural commodity firm StarAgri in a recent market intelligence report. > **"National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration now estimates a 67% probability of a "Super El Niño" this year, potentially the strongest on record."** ## El Niño Is Making Things Worse The culprit behind the erratic monsoon is a strengthening El Niño — the periodic warming of Pacific Ocean waters that disrupts weather patterns across South Asia. Japan's Meteorological Agency confirmed an El Niño event in mid-June, and the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration now estimates a 67% probability of a "Super El Niño" this year, potentially the strongest on record. History offers little comfort. Since 1951, twelve out of seventeen El Niño years have coincided with below-normal or deficient rainfall in India. The El Niño is expected to peak toward the end of 2026 and persist until March 2027, raising the prospect of a prolonged drought that could affect not just kharif but also the winter rabi crop season. The India Meteorological Department has forecast July rainfall at below 94% of the long-period average — a significant downgrade from earlier projections. While a positive Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) may partly offset the damage, analysts at NSE Market Pulse cautioned that the IOD failed to prevent a 13.7% rainfall deficit in 2015, highlighting the potential severity of the current situation. ## Food Inflation Is Already Creeping Up The supply-side shock is visible in price data. Current retail prices of cooking oils are 12-17% higher year-on-year. Tomato and onion prices have spiked 23% and 11% respectively. A prolonged monsoon shortfall could push these numbers higher, particularly for non-cereal crops like oilseeds, pulses, and vegetables.

India does have a buffer: government-held rice stocks are at record highs, up 15% from a year ago, thanks to consecutive years of good monsoons in 2024 and 2025. But that cushion doesn't extend to pulses, oilseeds, and cotton, where India remains dependent on imports. The global picture adds another layer of concern. The UN's Food and Agriculture Organization warned this week that El Niño threatens sugar, palm oil, and cereal production across multiple regions. Below-average Indian monsoon rains have already boosted global sugar prices. India's own sugar industry body, ISMA, has revised its production forecast downward. ## What This Means for the Diaspora For NRIs sending money home to families in rural India, a bad monsoon translates directly into higher food bills and economic stress. India received over $120 billion in remittances in 2025, the highest in the world — and a significant portion flows to households in agrarian states like Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Maharashtra, and Madhya Pradesh, precisely the regions most exposed to rainfall deficits. When agricultural output is low, these families' primary income sources are hit, increasing their reliance on financial support from abroad. This could mean NRIs might need to send larger or more frequent remittances to help their families cope with increased expenses for food and other necessities. There's also a trade dimension. India accounts for roughly 40% of global rice exports. In past El Niño droughts, the government has restricted grain exports to protect domestic supplies. Any repeat of those curbs would affect rice availability and prices across the Middle East, Africa, and Southeast Asia — regions home to large Indian diaspora communities. This could impact the cost of staple foods for NRIs living in these regions, or for those who regularly send food supplies back home. ## The Next Two Weeks Are Critical Agricultural experts say the window for recovery is narrow but not yet closed. July contributes more than 32% of total monsoon rainfall. If the monsoon gains momentum in the first half of July, farmers can still plant most kharif crops within the viable window. But if the dry spell stretches past mid-July, crop area — and ultimately yields — will be significantly lower.

"A recovery in rainfall by mid-July will aid kharif planting, but any further delay in sowing will mean a loss of yields," said Amith Agarwal, CEO of StarAgri. India's weather department has forecast a modest improvement in rainfall patterns over the coming days. Whether the skies deliver will determine not just one growing season, but the trajectory of food prices, rural demand, and economic growth for the rest of 2026, with direct implications for the financial well-being of millions of families connected to the Indian diaspora.
